newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan rates seen steady after weak economic data.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan rates seen steady after weak economic data.

text.p: Taiwan's central bank, which investors feared would try to tighten liquidity to cool the stock market, is likely to leave interest rates unchanged after disappointing February economic data, analysts said on Thursday.

The Economics Ministry said on Thursday that foreign orders for Taiwan goods fell 1.7 percent to US$8.697 billion in February compared to February 1996, a worse showing than the average forecast 0.45 percent downturn from a March 18 Reuters Poll of Taiwan economists.
February industrial output rose just 0.55 percent over the year-earlier, far below an average forecast 7.31 percent rise.

"The flat performance should ease worries that the central bank might raise interest rates to tighten liquidity simply because of the red-hot stock market," said Grand Cathay Securities vice-president Terry Chen.
"The trend of a slowly recovering economy hasn't changed, and the central bank likely will continue its stable-to-loose monetary policy to help boost the economy," Chen said.
Taiwan' stock index on Thursday ended 51.15 points higher at 8,492.67. It has already risen some 23 percent in 1997.
The ministry's chief statistician, Chang Yao-tsung, attributed the disappointing industrial showing to fewer working days this February than last year, and lower export prices.
There were only 17.5 working days in February 1997 compared to 19 in February 1996.
Economists admitted failing to take into account an extra February holiday in 1997 when making their forecasts.
Taiwan's parliament declared February 28 a national holiday to mark the day in 1947 when Nationalists troops fleeing China's communists gunned down thousands of Taiwanese civilians.
The decision, which came just three days before the actual holiday, drew protests from business leaders who warned of lost productivity.
"Since February 28 was an unexpected holiday, we should not judge the overall economy simply by using February's figures," said Nomura Securities economist Amy Huang.
"We should wait to see if March's industrial output can resume its recent fairly strong growth of more than five percent," Huang said.
Chang said the volume of export orders in Taiwan's two leading export sectors, information technology and electronics, actually rose in February compared to February 1996.
But a sharp 10 percent fall in average prices in those sectors contributed to a decline in the value of overall orders, Chang said.
Nomura's Huang added that sluggish exports for the first quarter had been predicted.
"We will not see apparent recovery in exports until the second quarter," Huang said.
The real estate and construction industries saw a sharp drop in output, falling 47.57 percent from a year ago.

Chang said a year-on-year rise of 7.27 percent in the land area which construction firms have sought for development permits indicated that the long-sluggish sector would see a clear rebound in the second half of 1997.
